tldr: We identified an overlooked cause of offline-to-online RL instability: the entropy term turning negative. By introducing a sigmoid-bounded entropy that stays strictly positive, our proposed method stabilizes and accelerates training without collapsing, even with a single demonstration and across four real-world robot platforms.
hero_caption: Comparison between standard entropy and the proposed Sigmoid-Bounded Entropy (SigEnt). (a) Standard Gaussian entropy locally depresses the objective function near the policy mean, while SigEnt stays strictly positive and bounded, avoiding distortion of the Q-function landscape. (b) A diagnostic metric measuring the accelerative oscillation of policy updates shows that the violent oscillations seen in existing methods are dramatically suppressed with SigEnt.
overview:
Offline-to-online reinforcement learning initializes a policy with pre-collected offline data and refines skills through online trial-and-error in real environments. It is seen as a key solution to lower interaction costs for real-world robotics. However, in data-scarce regimes—such as one-shot learning from a single demonstration—training has long suffered from severe value estimation instability, where Q-values oscillate violently or diverge, causing learning to collapse. Prior countermeasures like pessimistic penalties and LayerNorm have helped, but they fail to resolve the root issue.

The authors discovered that this overlooked root cause lies within the entropy calculation itself in maximum entropy RL. In $\tanh$-squashed Gaussian policies used in methods like SAC, sample probability density can become locally high, causing the sample-wise entropy contribution (typically $-\log \pi$) to take negative values. When added to the Q-function, this pulls the policy mean unnaturally. As the policy shifts, it queries the Critic on different actions, further destabilizing value estimation in a vicious cycle.

To address this, the authors developed SCQ (Sigmoid-Bounded Conservative Q-Learning), which smoothly bounds the entropy contribution to a positive $[0, 1]$ range using a logistic sigmoid function. After proving that it preserves theoretical contraction mapping properties, they confirmed via clipping intervention experiments (removing the negative branch) that keeping the term strictly positive is the true driver of stability. Across benchmark tasks and single-demonstration settings, as well as four entirely different real-robot platforms (manipulator, wheeled, quadruped, and humanoid), SCQ succeeded in visual task learning from a single local camera, demonstrating remarkable generalization and stability.
contributions: Identified the sample-wise negative entropy phenomenon in $\tanh$-squashed Gaussian policies as an overlooked source of RL update instability.

Proposed a sigmoid-bounded entropy (SigEnt) that keeps the entropy contribution strictly positive and bounded, integrating it with conservative Q-learning (Cal-QL) and Critic-only LayerNorm to form SCQ.
Demonstrated through clipping intervention experiments that removing negative values is key to stabilization, and theoretically proved convergence to a unique fixed point under idealized backups.
Achieved higher stability and superior success rates over baselines on D4RL benchmarks, single-demonstration learning, and four real-robot platforms (manipulator, wheeled, quadruped, humanoid).

sections.heading: Why does RL suddenly collapse? The overlooked trap of negative entropy
sections.summary: We analyzed why value estimation becomes unstable when transitioning from offline data in real-world robot RL. The results show that a negative standard entropy term distorts the policy update direction, triggering a vicious cycle with value estimation, which SCQ successfully resolves.
sections.details:
When teaching robots skills in the real world, learning from scratch with RL carries prohibitive trial-and-error costs. Offline-to-online RL has emerged as a promising alternative, warm-starting policy training with offline data like human demonstrations before exploring online. Prior methods like Cal-QL and RLPD introduced conservative penalties to prevent Q-value overestimation and used normalization (LayerNorm) for stability. However, under extreme conditions such as having only a single demonstration, policies still suffer from severe oscillations and training collapses.

The authors point out that the root of this instability lies in the entropy formulation itself. Maximum entropy RL algorithms like SAC commonly use Gaussian policies squashed by $\tanh$ to bound actions within $[-1, 1]$. When the probability density becomes locally concentrated, the sample-wise entropy contribution $-\log \pi(a|s)$ turns negative. Instead of acting as an exploration bonus, entropy ends up depressing the objective function and distorting the update direction of the policy mean. As the policy moves unnaturally, the Critic is queried at shifted action positions. The resulting distorted Q-values further corrupt the next policy update, creating a destructive feedback loop.

The proposed SCQ (Sigmoid-Bounded Conservative Q-Learning) builds upon Cal-QL and replaces the entropy contribution with a strictly positive bounded score (SigEnt) using a logistic sigmoid function. This prevents entropy from warping the Q-function landscape, achieving smooth and stable policy improvement even under data scarcity.

sections.heading: Where do prior methods fall short, and how does SCQ fit in?
sections.summary: We review three related fields: offline-to-online RL, entropy regularization, and real-world robot RL. Rather than relying on massive pretrained models (VLAs), SCQ fundamentally improves the stability of the underlying RL solver itself.
sections.details:
This work sits at the intersection of three major research areas:

### II-A Offline-to-Online Reinforcement Learning
To warm-start policies with offline data and transition to online fine-tuning, methods such as IQL, CQL, AWAC, and TD3+BC have been proposed. Cal-QL calibrates Q-values using Monte Carlo return lower bounds to smooth this transition, while RLPD curbs overestimation using large Critic ensembles and LayerNorm. However, most prior work assumes abundant data, leaving visual-input, extreme data-scarcity (few-shot) real-world settings under-explored.

### II-B Entropy-Regularized Policy Optimization
In maximum entropy RL, typified by SAC, entropy balances exploration and exploitation. While past studies modified entropy formulations for sparse control or richer expressiveness, none examined the specific pitfalls of negative sample-wise entropy in conservative offline-to-online learning.

### II-C Reinforcement Learning for Real-World Robotics
Real-robot RL faces safety constraints and sample-efficiency bottlenecks. Approaches like HIL-SERL incorporate human interventions, while others like RLT and EXPO-FT leverage pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models as feature extractors or action priors. However, these methods are often validated only on single-arm precision manipulation tasks without demonstrating transfer across diverse robot morphologies like quadrupeds or humanoids. The authors argue that before relying on heavy backbones like VLAs, we must fix the estimation instabilities inherent to the RL algorithm itself.

sections.heading: How Sigmoid-Bounded Entropy (SigEnt) works and its theoretical guarantees
sections.summary: Applying a sigmoid function keeps entropy strictly positive, which is integrated with automatic temperature tuning and Cal-QL conservative penalties. We theoretically prove that the Q-function retains its contraction mapping property under idealized backups, converging to a unique fixed point.
sections.details:
The core of SCQ is simple yet effective: make entropy strictly positive and bounded.

### IV-A Mechanism of Sigmoid-Bounded Entropy (SigEnt)
Let the action space be normalized to $[-1, 1]^{d_a}$, using a $\tanh$-squashed Gaussian policy. Defining the surprise for dimension $i$ as $\ell_i = -\log \pi_{\theta, i}(a_i|s)$, standard RL allows $\ell_i$ to turn negative. SCQ applies the logistic sigmoid function $\operatorname{sigmoid}(u) = (1 + e^{-u})^{-1}$ to define bounded entropy as:
$$\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{sig}}(s, a; \theta) = h_{\max} \sum_{i=1}^{d_a} \operatorname{sigmoid}\left(\frac{\ell_i - m}{t}\right)$$
Here, $h_{\max}=1$ is normalized, with center $m=-0.3$ and scale $t=0.55$. This guarantees the entropy contribution stays strictly within $(0, d_a h_{\max})$ and never drops below zero.

### IV-B Policy and Temperature Parameter Learning
The policy (Actor) balances maximizing Q-values and maximizing SigEnt (minimizing the corresponding loss). The temperature parameter $\alpha > 0$ automatically tunes the entropy weight to track a target entropy $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{target}} \approx 0.25743 d_a$, derived from a target standard deviation $\sigma_{\mathrm{tar}} = 0.1$.

### IV-C Critic Learning and Network Architecture
The Critic's TD error target incorporates $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{sig}}$ instead of standard $-\log \pi$. Additionally, Cal-QL conservative loss is applied: it penalizes policy-sampled actions from receiving undeserved high Q-values while anchoring them to Monte Carlo return lower bounds from the offline buffer. Following RLPD, LayerNorm is applied strictly to Critic networks to prevent gradient explosions (Actor networks remain unnormalized).

### IV-D Theoretical Properties: Contraction Mapping and Scale Equivariance
In theoretical analysis, the idealized fixed-policy backup operator with SigEnt is proven to be a $\gamma$-contraction in the supremum norm space of Q-functions (Theorem 1). This guarantees that exact Q-iteration converges to a unique fixed point. Furthermore, Theorem 2 proves scale equivariance: changing $h_{\max}$ while adjusting the target entropy leaves the stationary solution unchanged, providing solid theoretical ground without delicate hyperparameter tuning.

sections.heading: Did eliminating negative values make the difference? Validation on benchmarks and four real robots
sections.summary: Clipping experiments that zero out only the negative entropy branch verified the core hypothesis. Extensive evaluations on D4RL benchmarks, single-demo learning, and four real-robot platforms (manipulator, wheeled, quadruped, humanoid) proved that SCQ prevents collapse and achieves high success rates.
sections.details:
The experiments in this paper range from validating underlying mechanisms to full real-robot deployment.

### V-B Direct Mechanism Validation: Positivity is Key (Q1)
To test whether the sigmoid curve shape or non-negativity was the primary driver, the authors evaluated a direct clipping intervention: $H_{\mathrm{clip}} = \sum_i \max(0, -\log \pi_i)$, which zeroes out negative values while preserving positive ones. Under the single-demonstration protocol (Table III), standard entropy yielded an average AUC of 0.485 and 3,072 online successes. Removing the negative branch via clipping increased AUC to 0.532 and successes to 3,899. SigEnt pushed this further to AUC 0.581 and 4,299 successes. Gradient-matched controls like ReLU and Softplus showed similar gains, confirming that eliminating negative entropy contributions is the primary driver of performance.

### V-C Standard Benchmarks and Anatomy of Training Collapse (Q2, Q3)
On 13 D4RL tasks (Table I), SCQ was compared against Cal-QL, RLPD, and FlashSAC (RSS 2026 Best Paper). Cal-QL collapsed to zero performance midway on Adroit and Kitchen tasks, whereas SCQ maintained stable high scores. In Relocate task diagnostics (Figure 3), standard entropy saw negative entropy fractions reach ~48% around 30k steps, triggering violent policy gradient swings and numeric Critic divergence near 38k steps. SCQ completely averted this failure, reaching ~76% success at 1M steps. It also demonstrated competitive visual control across 8 Visual DMC tasks (Figure 4).

### V-D & V-E Single-Demo Learning and Four Real-Robot Platforms (Q4, Q5)
SCQ learned stable policies even when initialized with only a single successful demonstration. Furthermore, real-robot monocular visual control tests (Table V) across four platforms showed remarkable results:
- **Precision Alignment (Robot Arm)**: Reached ~0.2 mm target accuracy with 10/10 successes (VSAC: 10/10, HIL-SERL: 15/15).
- **Wheeled Robot Ball Pocketing**: Pushed a ball into a goal from unseen layouts with 6/10 successes (VSAC: 2/10, HIL-SERL: 1/10).
- **Quadruped Slalom Navigation**: Navigated around dynamic obstacle layouts with 8/10 successes (VSAC: 4/10, HIL-SERL: 4/10).
- **Humanoid Walk & Kick**: Walked from arbitrary positions, avoided obstacles, and kicked a ball into the goal with 10/10 successes (VSAC: 3/10).

Online interaction was kept minimal (20k–30k steps, up to 150k on the humanoid). Achieving these results purely by stabilizing the core RL algorithm without pretrained VLAs is a standout outcome.

sections.heading: Conclusions and outlook: Towards low-level joint control and long-horizon tasks
sections.summary: SCQ prevents RL collapse and delivers exceptional real-world stability by keeping entropy strictly positive via sigmoid bounding. Acknowledged limitations include testing low-level torque control and addressing very long-horizon tasks.
sections.details:
### Acknowledged Limitations
The authors identify several limitations of this work:
- **Control Abstraction Level**: The system uses 4-DoF end-effector position commands for precision alignment and high-level velocity commands for the humanoid, rather than low-level, full-body joint-level torque control.
- **Task Horizon**: Real-robot experiments focus on distinct, focused skills like alignment and slalom kicking. Evaluating contact-rich, multi-stage, long-horizon task composition remains future work.

### Conclusion
SCQ eliminates policy update oscillation and value estimation collapse by replacing standard log-probability entropy with a strictly positive sigmoid-bounded score (SigEnt). Backed by contraction mapping convergence guarantees and empirical validation showing that removing negative entropy contributions is key, SCQ presents a powerful foundational technique for sample-efficient and stable real-world robot reinforcement learning.

sections.heading: Mathematical proofs and parameter design formulas
sections.summary: Details on the Cal-QL style conservative loss formula, the full contraction mapping proof for fixed-policy backups, and calculations showing that the sigmoid shape is optimally placed in the policy sensitivity region.
sections.details:
### Appendix A: Conservative Regularization on the Critic
For state $s$ sampled from the replay buffer, candidate actions $\mathcal{A}_{\pi}(s)$ are drawn from the current policy. Calibrated values $\widetilde{Q}$ anchored to Monte Carlo returns lower-bound these actions, penalized via a log-sum-exp formulation against buffer actions. This yields the conservative loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CQL}}$ in Eq. (18), preventing unvisited actions from acquiring undeservedly high Q-values.

### Appendix B & C: Outline of Theorem Proofs
In the proof of Theorem 1, evaluating the difference between two Critic ensembles $\mathbf{Q}$ and $\widetilde{\mathbf{Q}}$ reveals that the entropy term $\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{sig}}$ cancels out since it does not depend on Q. Because the finite ensemble minimum $\min_i Q_i$ is non-expansive, the TD target difference is bounded by $\gamma \|\mathbf{Q} - \widetilde{\mathbf{Q}}\|_{\infty}$, proving convergence to a unique fixed point via Banach's Fixed Point Theorem. Theorem 2 algebraically demonstrates that stationary conditions (gradient = 0) are invariant under scale transformations.

### Appendix D: Sensitivity Analysis for Sigmoid Parameters $(m, t)$
The shape parameters $(m, t) = (-0.3, 0.55)$ are derived analytically. Evaluating the expected surprise of the pre-squashed Gaussian policy shows that the standard deviation interval where the sigmoid derivative retains over 80% of peak sensitivity is $\sigma \in [0.105, 0.304]$. The target standard deviation $\sigma_{\mathrm{tar}} = 0.1$ lies right at the boundary of this active region, avoiding saturation zones (vanishing gradients) and ensuring well-behaved policy entropy control.

takeaways: When using $\tanh$-squashed Gaussian policies in RL, always check if sample-wise entropy becomes negative and destabilizes policy updates.
Clipping or bounding entropy contributions into a strictly positive range via sigmoid functions dramatically suppresses optimization oscillations and Q-value divergence.

Without relying on massive pretrained models (VLAs), improving the intrinsic stability of the RL algorithm enables visual policy transfer to diverse robot morphologies from a single demonstration and minimal real-world interaction.
limitations: The humanoid and manipulator experiments rely on higher-level Cartesian position or velocity commands rather than low-level, direct joint torque control.
Has not yet been validated on ultra long-horizon, multi-stage tasks with rich and complex contacts.
